cds.text: Understand that compound sentences link two or more independent clauses, usually with a coordinating conjunction, to connect ideas
Understand that a clause is a unit of grammar, usually with a subject and verb that must agree
Understand that complex sentences have one independent clause and at least one dependent clause, joined by subordinating conjunctions to show time and cause
Understand that nouns can extend into noun groups with articles and adjectives, and verbs can form verb groups
Understand how verbs represent processes of doing, feeling, thinking, saying and relating
Investigate how quoted (direct) and reported (indirect) speech are used
Understand that verbs are anchored in time through tense
Understand how adverb groups and prepositional phrases give circumstantial details about an activity
Understand past, present and future tenses and their impact on meaning in a sentence
Recognise capitals in titles and commas separating items in lists
Understand apostrophes for contractions and for singular and plural possession
Understand quotation marks signal dialogue, dialogue capitalisation conventions, and commas and boundary punctuation
Manipulate more complex sounds in spoken words, using blending, segmenting, phoneme deletion and substitution to read and write words
Use short and common long vowels, consonant blends and digraphs to write and blend words; read consonant clusters and silent letters in words of one or more syllables, including compound words
Blend and segment to read and write multisyllabic words with more complex letter patterns fluently
Read and write words with more complex letter combinations, including a variety of vowel sounds and known prefixes and suffixes
Use spelling patterns and morphemes to read and write words not fully predictable from sounds, including high-frequency words
Apply common base words, prefixes, suffixes and suffix-adding generalisations to read and understand new multimorphemic words
Use letter patterns (including double letters), spelling generalisations, word families, prefixes, suffixes and word origins to spell more complex words
Build morphemic word families using knowledge of prefixes and suffixes
Use phoneme-grapheme relationships and less common letter patterns to spell words
Recognise and write most high-frequency words, including some homophones
Read and write high-frequency words, including homophones, and use context to identify correct spelling

sentences.text: {{S}} automatically uses strategies in a range of contexts to spell unfamiliar words.
{{S}} identifies complex letter patterns and sounds when spelling and applies this knowledge to improve spelling accuracy.
{{S}} applies spelling generalisations to spell most familiar and less common words correctly.
{{S}} selects appropriate tenses to suit different writing tasks.
{{S}} applies familiar spelling patterns and is working towards greater accuracy when spelling less common words.
{{S}} spells familiar words by using common letter patterns and recognising the sounds in words.
{{S}} checks {{pos}} work for spelling mistakes and uses dictionaries to correct them.
{{S}} uses commas to separate parts of a sentence and apostrophes for contractions.
{{S}} varies sentence length to improve {{pos}} writing.

rows.newText: {{S}} writes sentences with a clear clause that has a subject and a verb that agree.
{{S}} identifies the subject and the verb in a clause and checks that they agree.
{{S}} uses verbs that show doing, feeling, thinking, saying and relating.
{{S}} chooses verbs to describe what characters do, feel, think and say.
{{S}} uses verb tense to show when something happens.
{{S}} keeps the tense of verbs consistent throughout a piece of writing.
{{S}} uses apostrophes for contractions and for singular and plural possession.
{{S}} blends and segments sounds to read and write longer words with more complex letter patterns.
{{S}} spells multisyllabic words by breaking them into sounds and syllables.
{{S}} applies base words, prefixes, suffixes and suffix-adding rules to spell and understand words.
{{S}} uses base words and common endings to work out the meaning of new words.
{{S}} uses sound and letter relationships and less common letter patterns to spell words.
{{S}} recognises and writes most high-frequency words, including some homophones.
{{S}} chooses the correct homophone, such as there and their, when writing.
{{S}} writes complex sentences with one main clause and at least one dependent clause.
{{S}} uses linking words such as because, although and when to build complex sentences.
{{S}} uses quoted speech and reported speech correctly in {{pos}} writing.
{{S}} explains the difference between direct and reported speech.
{{S}} adds detail to sentences using adverb groups and prepositional phrases.
{{S}} uses words such as quickly, in the morning and near the river to say how, when and where.
{{S}} uses past, present and future tense and knows how tense changes meaning.
{{S}} uses quotation marks and capitals correctly when writing dialogue.
{{S}} starts a new line for each speaker when writing dialogue.
{{S}} reads and writes words with complex letter combinations, including a variety of vowel sounds.
{{S}} spells words with double letters, word families, prefixes and suffixes.
{{S}} uses spelling generalisations and word families to spell new words.
{{S}} reads and writes high-frequency words and homophones, using context to choose the correct spelling.
{{S}} uses the meaning of a sentence to select the correct homophone.
{{S}} reads and spells words with complex letter combinations and different vowel sounds.
